etymology: Short for fan fiction: stories written by fans using the characters and worlds of someone else’s books, films, or games. Modern fan fiction grew out of 1960s Star Trek fanzines (Spockanalia, 1967, is the usual first example), moved online in the 1990s (FanFiction.Net opened in 1998), and became a mass hobby with Archive of Our Own (2008), Wattpad, and Tumblr. Fanfic and fic are the everyday clipped forms.
biblical_def: In current slang fanfic is fan-written fiction — a teenager takes the characters of a favourite series and writes what happens next, what might have happened, or what the author never would have allowed. Millions of young people write and read it, and some of them are learning to write well. The Christian observation: imagination is a gift of the God who made man in His own image, and story is one of the ways the Bible itself teaches (the parables are fiction with a point). But fanfic carries two dangers. The first is moral: the archives hold a vast amount of romantic and explicit material, often pairing characters in ways their authors never wrote, behind thin warnings a child clicks straight through. Paul gives the filter: "whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely... think on these things" (Php 4:8). The second is the habit of mind. Fanfic trains a reader to treat every story as raw material to be rewritten to taste; carried into the Bible, that habit becomes the sin Proverbs forbids: "Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar" (Pro 30:6). The apostles insisted they had not followed "cunningly devised fables" but were "eyewitnesses of his majesty" (2Pe 1:16). A father tells his daughter: write stories, and write them well; keep your imagination clean, "bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ" (2Co 10:5); and never write fanfic of the one Book that is not fiction.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (1960s Star Trek fanzines; online from the 1990s; a mass hobby since c. 2008) for fiction fans write in someone else’s story world — a real creative gift that must be kept pure, and a rewriting habit that must never touch the Word of God.
webster_full: FANFIC, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 1990s–present; fandom origin) A story written by a fan using the characters or world of an existing book, film, show, or game. "I stayed up till two reading a fanfic about the side characters."
Fic, n., the short form. Tags such as AU (alternate universe) and ship (a paired romance) sort the stories; fanon is what fans have collectively decided beyond the source.
Older relatives know the thing without the word: pastiche, sequels by other hands, the endless "further adventures" of Sherlock Holmes.

Webster (1828), root word fiction: “FIC'TION, noun […] 1. The act of feigning, inventing or imagining; as, by the mere fiction of the mind. 2. That which is feigned, invented or imagined. The story is a fiction So also was the fiction of those golden apples kept by a dragon, taken from the serpent which tempted Eve.”
Decode for parents: fanfic archives mix wholesome stories with explicit ones under the same beloved characters. Ask to see what your child reads and writes.
scriptures: Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Pro 30:6
Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.
corruption_summary: Fanfic exercises a God-given imagination, but its archives are thick with impurity, and its core habit — rewriting someone else’s story to taste — is fatal when it is turned on Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Writing in a borrowed world is an old apprenticeship; plenty of good writers learned their craft by imitating the books they loved. The trouble is what fills the archives. Much fanfic exists to do what the original author would not: pair characters romantically, sexualize them, or drag them into darkness for the thrill of it. A child searching for more of a beloved story can be three clicks from material no parent would allow in the house. Paul’s rule is not a ban on imagination but a direction for it: "whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely... think on these things" (Php 4:8). Every imagined scene is to be brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ (2Co 10:5).

The quieter danger is the habit. Fanfic teaches that the reader is the final authority over the story: if you dislike the ending, write a better one. That is fine with a novel and deadly with the Bible, where many have done exactly that — trimming the hard sayings, adding a gentler Jesus, inventing what the text never says. "Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar" (Pro 30:6). Paul told Timothy to refuse old wives’ fables (1Ti 4:7); Peter said the gospel is no set of "cunningly devised fables" (2Pe 1:16). Teach your children the difference between a story they may reshape and the one they must receive.
roots_summary: Fan (from fanatic) + fiction → 1960s Star Trek fanzines → 1990s internet archives → fanfic, fic, a mass Gen-Z hobby.
roots_lines: Latin fanaticus — of a temple, frenzied; English fan, an enthusiast (late 1800s baseball)
Latin fictio — a making, a fashioning; English fiction
1967: Spockanalia, an early Star Trek fanzine printing fan stories
1998 FanFiction.Net; 2008 Archive of Our Own; Wattpad and Tumblr
Gen-Z: fic, AU, ship, canon vs. fanon
usage: "The show ended badly so I’m just reading fanfic where it didn’t."
Write stories; never rewrite the Word (Pro 30:6).
Bring every imagined thought into captivity to Christ (2Co 10:5).

etymology: From Old English lār, teaching, learning (kin to learn). Fantasy fiction and video games (the Elder Scrolls and Dark Souls series are the usual examples) used lore for the backstory of an invented world, often hidden in item descriptions for players to piece together. In the early 2020s TikTok turned the word on people: a person’s lore is his backstory, and a lore drop is a revealing story from his past ("the lore runs deep").
biblical_def: In current slang lore is backstory — the hidden history of a game world, or, more and more, of a person: "wait, what’s the lore?" means "how did this happen?" and a lore drop is an old story that suddenly explains someone. The Christian observation: this is one of the most redeemable words in the language, because Christianity has the deepest lore of all, and God commands that it be told. Israel was to answer the child’s question: "when thy son asketh thee in time to come, saying, What mean the testimonies" (Deu 6:20). The psalmist made it a family duty: "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD" (Psa 78:4), and the next generation sang it back: "our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days" (Psa 44:1). When the lore is not passed down, the result is the book of Judges: "there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD" (Jdg 2:10). Paul adds the one warning: not every backstory edifies; give no heed to "fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions" (1Ti 1:4). A father tells his son: you know the lore of your favourite game down to the last item description; learn the lore of your own family and your own church, the true story of what God has done, and be ready to tell it to your children.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (fantasy and video-game backstory; applied to people on TikTok, early 2020s) for the hidden history behind a world or a person — and the faith has the deepest lore of all, which fathers are commanded to tell (Psa 78:4).
webster_full: LORE, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; gaming and fandom origin) The backstory of a game, a series, or a person. "Okay but what’s the lore behind you and your cousin not talking?"
Lore drop, a revealing story from someone’s past. Deep lore, obscure backstory only devoted fans know. "The lore thickens."
Older sense, still current: learning or teaching handed down, as folklore, sea lore, the lore of the elders.

Webster (1828), root word lore: “LORE, noun Learning; doctrine; lesson; instruction. The law of nations, or the lore of war. Lo! Rome herself, proud mistress now no more of arts, but thundering against heathen lore”
Decode for parents: your teen is asking for the story behind things. Tell them God’s, and your family’s.
scriptures: Deu 6:20
And when thy son asketh thee in time to come, saying, What mean the testimonies, and the statutes, and the judgments, which the LORD our God hath commanded you?
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Psa 44:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, Maschil. We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old.
Jdg 2:10
And also all that generation were gathered unto their fathers: and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel.
Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do.
corruption_summary: Lore is an honest word for backstory with little corruption of its own; the drift is a generation that knows a game’s lore by heart and the lore of the LORD not at all.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with enjoying a well-built story world. The trouble is proportion. A boy can explain the hidden history of a video game across three sequels and cannot tell you who Gideon was or why his grandfather joined the church he did. That is not an accident; whoever tells the stories forms the child. The book of Judges shows what a nation looks like one generation after the lore stopped being told: "there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel" (Jdg 2:10).

God’s answer is the family table. The Passover was built around a child’s question (Deu 6:20); the stones at the Jordan were set up so that children would ask what they meant (Jos 4:6). Paul’s warning keeps it honest: not all backstory edifies, and "endless genealogies" and speculation can crowd out faith (1Ti 1:4). Tell the true lore — creation, fall, redemption, and the works of God in your own family — and tell it until your children can tell it back to theirs (Psa 78:4).
roots_summary: Old English lār (teaching) → lore, knowledge handed down → fantasy and game backstory → early-2020s TikTok: a person’s lore, a lore drop.
roots_lines: Old English lār — teaching, instruction; kin to learn
Modern English: folklore, bird lore, knowledge passed down
20th-c. fantasy fiction: the invented history of a world
2000s–2010s video games: backstory hidden in item text and ruins
Early 2020s TikTok: a person’s lore; the lore drop
usage: "Wait, you used to live in Alaska? Huge lore drop."
Tell your children the lore of the LORD (Psa 78:4).
One generation without the lore, and you get Judges 2:10.

etymology: From canon, which fandom borrowed from the church: early-1900s Sherlock Holmes enthusiasts called Conan Doyle’s stories "the Canon," and later fandoms used canon for whatever the original author actually wrote. A headcanon (canon that exists only in one’s head) is a fan’s private interpretation — a detail, motive, or relationship never stated in the source. The word appears in online fandom in the 2000s and became common on Tumblr in the early 2010s.
biblical_def: In current slang a headcanon is a fan’s private belief about a story that the story never states: this character is secretly afraid of the dark, those two were really friends all along. Fans know the difference between canon (what the author wrote) and headcanon (what they wish or imagine), and that distinction is the most useful thing about the word. The Christian observation: canon was the church’s word before it was fandom’s. The canon of Scripture is the rule God has given, closed and sufficient, and the Christian life depends on keeping it separate from our headcanon. Peter says it plainly: "no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation" (2Pe 1:20). Moses draws the line: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children" (Deu 29:29). Paul tells the Corinthians "not to think of men above that which is written" (1Co 4:6), and Jeremiah condemns prophets who "speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD" (Jer 23:16). Much of the confusion in the church today is headcanon passed off as canon: "I just feel God would never..." A father tells his daughter: you may imagine all you like about a story someone made up; about God, stop where the Book stops, "and lean not unto thine own understanding" (Pro 3:5).
webster_summary: Gen-Z fandom slang (2000s; Tumblr, early 2010s) for a fan’s private interpretation of a story beyond what the source states — fair play with fiction, and a grave error with God, whose canon is closed (2Pe 1:20).
webster_full: HEADCANON, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2000s–present; fandom origin) A fan’s personal belief about a story or character that the original source does not state. "My headcanon is that he learned to cook from his grandma."
Contrasted with canon (what the author wrote) and fanon (a headcanon so widely shared that fans treat it as fact). "Headcanon accepted": I will believe it too.
Canon in the older sense a grandparent knows: the books received as Holy Scripture, the rule of faith; a church law; a standard.

Webster (1828), root word canon: “CANON, noun 1. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law, or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign; a decision of matters in religion, or a regulation of policy or discipline, by a general or provincial council. 2. A law or rule in general. 3.”
Decode for parents: your child already knows the difference between what the author said and what fans made up. Use it to teach the canon of Scripture.
scriptures: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.

And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
corruption_summary: Headcanon keeps an honest line between the author’s word and the reader’s imagination; the corruption is carrying headcanon into theology, where private interpretation is passed off as the Word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Fandom has accidentally preserved a Reformation principle. Every fan knows that the author’s text outranks the reader’s wish, and that a headcanon, however beloved, is not canon. That is exactly the line Scripture draws: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deu 29:29). What God has said binds the conscience; what we imagine He might say does not. Sola Scriptura is, among other things, a refusal to let anyone’s headcanon become the church’s canon.

The trouble is that many people who would never confuse fanon with canon in a television series do it constantly with God. A feeling about heaven, a guess about what Jesus would think of some modern sin, a preference about how God ought to judge — all of it is headcanon, and much of it contradicts the text. Peter forbids it: "no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation" (2Pe 1:20); Paul says not to go "above that which is written" (1Co 4:6). Teach your children to ask of every religious claim: is that canon, or somebody’s headcanon?
roots_summary: Greek kanōn (a measuring rod) → the church’s canon of Scripture → Sherlockian "the Canon" (1910s) → fandom canon → 2000s–2010s headcanon.
roots_lines: Greek kanōn — a straight rod, a rule or measure
Church Latin canon — the books received as Scripture; a rule of faith
1910s: Sherlock Holmes enthusiasts call Conan Doyle’s stories "the Canon"
Later fandoms: canon (official) vs. fanon (fan consensus)
2000s fandom, early-2010s Tumblr: headcanon, one fan’s private canon
usage: "It’s not in the books but it’s my headcanon and I’m keeping it."
No scripture is of any private interpretation (2Pe 1:20); God’s Book admits no headcanon.
Stop where the Book stops (Deu 29:29).

etymology: A fandom and critics’ term, current on internet forums and TV Tropes by the 2000s, for the invisible protection a main character enjoys because the story needs him alive: bullets miss, falls are survived, the villain monologues instead of finishing the job. Gen-Z applies it to real people too: a friend who walks away from every scrape "has plot armor."
biblical_def: In current slang plot armor is a character’s immunity to death or failure for story reasons: the hero cannot die in chapter three because the author needs him in chapter ten. Applied to people, it is a joke about someone who survives everything. The Christian observation: the joke is closer to theology than its users know. There is an Author, and His servants are kept until their work is done. Satan complained of Job’s protection: "Hast not thou made an hedge about him" (Job 1:10). Jesus walked through hostile crowds untouched; "no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come" (Joh 7:30). Paul was told in a sinking ship, "Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar" (Act 27:24). David confesses that every day was written before he lived it: "in thy book all my members were written" (Psa 139:16). But Scripture corrects the fiction in two places. First, God’s keeping is not immunity from suffering: Job lost everything, and the hedge was lowered for a purpose. Second, the armor comes off at the appointed time: "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Heb 9:27). Jesus had no plot armor at the cross; when His hour came, He laid His life down. A father tells his son: you are safe in God’s hand until your work is done, so be bold; and your work will be done one day, so be ready.
webster_summary: Gen-Z fandom slang (2000s forums; general in the 2010s) for a character’s story-given immunity to harm — a joke that half-sees providence: God’s servants are kept until their hour, and then appointed once to die (Heb 9:27).
webster_full: PLOT ARMOR, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2000s–present; fandom and criticism) The implausible protection a main character enjoys because the story needs him alive. "Ten guys shooting at him and not one hit? Plot armor."
Of real people: someone who survives every scrape, accident, or near-failing grade "has plot armor." Losing it: "his plot armor ran out."
Armor in the plain older sense: defensive covering for the body in battle; in Scripture, the whole armour of God (Eph 6:11).

Webster (1828), root word armor: “'ARMOR, noun […] 1. Defensive arms; any habit worn to protect the body in battle; formerly called harness. A complete armor formerly consisted of a casque or helmet, a gorget, cuirass, gauntlets, tasses, brassets, crushes, and covers for the legs to which the spurs were fastened.”
Decode for parents: a joke about invincibility. Teach the true version: kept by God until the work is done.
scriptures: Job 1:10
Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
Joh 7:30
Then they sought to take him: but no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come.
Saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.
Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
corruption_summary: Plot armor jokes about an author protecting his hero; the truth behind it is providence, and the corruption is presumption — treating God’s keeping as a guarantee against suffering or death.
corruption_paragraphs: Every reader knows the feeling: the hero is surrounded, and you are not worried, because there are two hundred pages left. Christians should recognize the shape. God is the Author of history, and His purposes are not frustrated by bullets or storms. Jesus walked out of the mob at Nazareth: "But he passing through the midst of them went his way" (Luk 4:30); no one could arrest Him "because his hour was not yet come" (Joh 7:30). An old missionary saying puts it well: a servant of God is immortal until his work is done.

The danger is presumption. Plot armor in fiction means the hero cannot be hurt; providence in Scripture means nothing touches the believer that God has not appointed — which includes the loss of Job’s children and the beheading of John the Baptist. And the keeping ends on schedule: "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Heb 9:27). A teenager who believes he has plot armor drives too fast. A teenager who believes in providence can be brave and careful at once, because his days are written in God’s book (Psa 139:16) and his Author is good.
roots_summary: Latin armatura (equipment) → English armor + plot (a story’s chain of events) → 2000s fandom plot armor → Gen-Z: a person who survives everything.
roots_lines: Latin armatura — arms, equipment; English armour, armor
English plot — a patch of ground, then a plan, then a storyline
2000s fan forums and TV Tropes: plot armor, protection the story grants
Kin to main character talk: the story bends around the hero
Gen-Z: real-life plot armor; "his plot armor ran out"
usage: "He fell off the garage roof and walked away. Actual plot armor."
Kept until his hour came (Joh 7:30) — providence, not plot armor.
The armor comes off on schedule: appointed once to die (Heb 9:27).

etymology: From role-playing games. Tabletop games such as Dungeons & Dragons (1974) and later video RPGs (The Legend of Zelda, The Elder Scrolls) divide a player’s tasks into the main quest, which advances the story, and optional side quests, which earn rewards along the way. Around 2021–2022 TikTok made side quest an everyday word for an unplanned detour: going out for milk and ending up helping a stranger move a couch.
biblical_def: In current slang a side quest is a diversion from the main task — sometimes a pointless distraction ("I was supposed to study but I went on a side quest about medieval spoons"), sometimes a delightful detour that became the best part of the day. The Christian observation: Scripture names both kinds. There is the side quest that steals the main one. Martha was busy with many things, and Jesus gently told her, "But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part" (Luk 10:42). Paul would not be pulled off course: "this one thing I do" (Php 3:13), and "No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life" (2Ti 2:4). "Let thine eyes look right on" (Pro 4:25). But there is also the side quest that was really the main quest in disguise. The priest and the Levite were too busy with their errands to stop; the Samaritan, "as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him" (Luk 10:33). His detour is the story Jesus told to define what loving a neighbour means. A father teaches his son to tell the two apart: the phone, the rabbit hole, the hobby that eats the homework are side quests to refuse; the hurting person God puts on your road is not a side quest at all.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (role-playing games; TikTok c. 2021–2022) for an unplanned diversion from the main task — Scripture warns against distractions that steal the one thing needful, and makes the Samaritan’s detour the main quest.
webster_full: SIDE QUEST, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2021–present; gaming origin) A diversion or detour from one’s main task, planned or not. "Went to get gas and ended up on a side quest to return a lost dog."
To go on a side quest; side-questing. Often self-mocking about procrastination; sometimes proud of an adventure.
In role-playing games: an optional mission apart from the main quest, which carries the story.

Webster (1828), root word quest: “QUEST, noun […] 1. The act of seeking; search; as, to rove in quest of game; to go in quest of a lost child; in quest of property, etc. 2. Inquest; a jury. […] 3. Searchers, collectively. […] 4. Inquiry; examination. […] 5. Request; desire; solicitation.”
Decode for parents: ask whether it was a distraction or a neighbour. One should be refused; the other may be God’s appointment.
scriptures: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
Php 3:13
Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,
No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
Pro 4:25
Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee.
But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,
corruption_summary: Side quest can dress up distraction as adventure; Scripture calls believers to the one thing needful, and also teaches that the neighbour in the ditch is never a detour.
corruption_paragraphs: A generation with a phone in its pocket lives on side quests. Every notification is an optional mission, and an hour of homework becomes four of clicking. Calling it a side quest makes the drift sound like an adventure, which is the oldest trick distraction has. Scripture’s answer is focus: Paul could say "this one thing I do" (Php 3:13), and he compared the Christian to a soldier who does not entangle himself with the affairs of this life (2Ti 2:4). Martha was not doing anything wicked; she was simply so busy with the side quests of hospitality that she missed the Guest (Luk 10:42).

Yet Jesus also told the story of a detour that was the whole point. The priest and the Levite stayed on task; the Samaritan stopped (Luk 10:33). The test is not whether the plan changed but whether love changed it. A rabbit hole that steals your duties is a side quest to refuse; the lonely kid at lunch, the widow who needs her gutters cleared, the stranger in the ditch are God’s appointments. Teach your children to let their eyes look right on (Pro 4:25) and to keep their hearts open to the ditch.
roots_summary: Latin quaerere (to seek) → English quest → tabletop and video RPGs: main quest vs. side quest → c. 2021–2022 TikTok: any detour from the plan.
roots_lines: Latin quaerere — to seek; Old French queste
Medieval romance: the knight’s quest, as for the Grail
1970s tabletop role-playing games; 1980s–2000s video RPGs
Side quest: an optional mission off the main storyline
c. 2021–2022 TikTok: real-life side quests
usage: "Was supposed to finish my essay, went on a two-hour side quest about sharks."
One thing is needful (Luk 10:42); refuse the side quests that steal it.
The Samaritan’s detour was the main quest (Luk 10:33).

etymology: The counterpart to side quest in role-playing games: the main quest is the central storyline a player must complete to finish the game. Gen-Z borrowed it in the early 2020s, often alongside main character talk, for the central task of a day or the chief purpose of a life ("okay, back to the main quest").
biblical_def: In current slang the main quest is the central task: the thing you are actually supposed to be doing, as opposed to the side quests. It is said of a day ("back to the main quest: laundry"), and sometimes of a life ("what’s even my main quest?"). That second question is a real one, and the culture’s answers are thin: find yourself, chase your dream, get the bag. The Christian observation: Scripture answers it plainly. The Preacher, having tried every side quest under the sun, writes the conclusion: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man" (Ecc 12:13). Jesus summed up the law: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind" (Mat 22:37). He set the order: "seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you" (Mat 6:33). He gave His church its standing commission: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations" (Mat 28:19). And Paul lived it as a race with a finish line: "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus" (Php 3:14). The Westminster Shorter Catechism puts it in one line a child can memorize: man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy Him for ever. A father tells his son: your job, your marriage, your sport are real quests, but they are not the main one; the main quest was handed to you by your Maker, and its reward is better than anything the game offers.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (role-playing games; general in the early 2020s) for one’s central task or purpose — a question Scripture answers outright: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of man (Ecc 12:13).
webster_full: MAIN QUEST, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2021–present; gaming origin) One’s central task, as opposed to side quests; one’s chief purpose. "Okay, enough scrolling, back to the main quest."
Often joking about small things (a chore, a test); sometimes earnest about life direction: "I don’t even know what my main quest is."
In role-playing games: the required storyline that leads to the end of the game.

Webster (1828), root word main: “MAIN, adjective […] 1. Principal; chief; that which has most power in producing an effect, or which is mostly regarded in prospect; as the main branch or tributary stream of a river; the main timbers of an edifice; a main design; a main object. Our main interest is to be as happy as we can, and as long as possible. 2. Mighty;”
Decode for parents: when your child asks what his main quest is, he is asking the first question of the catechism. Answer it.
scriptures: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
Mat 6:33
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Php 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Main quest rightly assumes a life has a central task; the drift is letting the self write it — career, fame, or self-discovery — when the Maker has already given it.
corruption_paragraphs: The game metaphor carries a hidden assumption the culture otherwise denies: someone else designed the quest. In a game no player invents the main storyline; he discovers it and follows it. The modern world tells young people to invent their own — to make the career, the following, or the self the main quest — and then wonders why so many feel aimless at twenty-five. The Preacher tried that route, called it vanity, and came at last to "the conclusion of the whole matter" (Ecc 12:13).

Scripture hands out the main quest by name: love God with all the heart, soul, and mind (Mat 22:37); seek first His kingdom (Mat 6:33); make disciples of all nations (Mat 28:19). Every other good thing — work, marriage, children, craft — is a real quest inside that one, and becomes an idol the moment it replaces it. Paul ran his life like a race with one finish line (Php 3:14). Teach your children the catechism early, so that when they ask what life is for, they already know the main quest.
roots_summary: Old English mægen (strength) → main (chief) + Latin-derived quest (a seeking) → RPG main quest → early-2020s Gen-Z: one’s central task or purpose.
roots_lines: Old English mægen — strength, might; English main, chief, principal
Latin quaerere — to seek; English quest
Role-playing games: the main quest, the required storyline
Early 2020s: main quest vs. side quest in everyday speech
Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647), Q. 1: the chief end of man
usage: "Senior year main quest: graduate. Everything else is a side quest."
The whole duty of man is the main quest (Ecc 12:13).
Seek first the kingdom; the rest is added (Mat 6:33).

etymology: Gaming slang that spread through Fortnite and Twitch around 2018–2019: a player who is cracked is so skilled he seems almost unfair ("he’s cracked at building"). The exact source is uncertain; it likely draws on older cracked up (praised, as in "not all it’s cracked up to be") and on slang for someone wired and frantic. The irony a grandparent will catch: in their usage cracked meant broken, or slightly crazy ("he’s a bit cracked").
biblical_def: In current slang someone who is cracked is extremely skilled, especially at a video game, but also at a sport, an instrument, or a subject: "she’s cracked at chess." It is high praise for skill that looks almost unfair. The Christian observation: Scripture honours skill. God filled Bezaleel "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship" (Exo 31:3); the young David was recommended to a king as "cunning in playing" (1Sa 16:18); Benjamin sent warriors who "could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones" (1Ch 12:2). "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). Skill is a gift and a stewardship. The questions are where it is spent and whom it serves. A boy can be cracked at a game that will be forgotten in five years and unpractised at everything that will matter in fifty. And the Preacher gives the humbling footnote: "the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong... nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all" (Ecc 9:11). A father tells his son: be cracked at something worth being good at, give God the credit for the hands He gave you, and remember that David’s skill with harp and sling served the LORD’s people, not a scoreboard.
webster_summary: Gen-Z gaming slang (Fortnite and Twitch, c. 2018–2019) for extreme skill — a gift Scripture honours in Bezaleel and David, given to be spent where it matters and credited to its Giver.
webster_full: CRACKED, adj. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2018–present; gaming origin) Extremely skilled; almost unfairly good. "Don’t queue against him, he’s cracked."
Cracked at a game, sport, or subject. Intensified: actually cracked, lowkey cracked.
Older senses a grandparent knows: split or broken ("a cracked cup"); slightly crazy ("he’s a bit cracked"); not all it’s cracked up to be.

Webster (1828), root word crack: “CRACK, verb transitive 1. To rend, break, or burst into chinks; to break partially; to divide the parts a little from each other; as, to crack a board or a rock; or to break without an entire severance of the parts; as, to crack glass, or ice. 2. To break in pieces; as, to crack nuts. 3. To break with grief; to affect deeply; to pain;”
Decode for parents: a compliment for skill. Ask what the skill is for.
scriptures: Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,

Then answered one of the servants, and said, Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the LORD is with him.
They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
Ecc 9:11

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
corruption_summary: Cracked praises real skill, which Scripture honours; the drift is spending a gift on what will not last, and taking the glory for hands God made.
corruption_paragraphs: Skill is a biblical good. The tabernacle was built by craftsmen the Spirit of God had filled (Exo 31:3), and the man diligent in his business stands before kings (Pro 22:29). There is nothing wrong with a boy who has put ten thousand hours into his reflexes. The question Scripture presses is stewardship: ten thousand hours is a decade of afternoons, and it can be spent on a game that will be patched out of existence or on a trade, an instrument, a language, a body trained for work.

The second danger is pride. A player who is cracked is easily worshipped by his lobby and easily convinced the skill is his own. Paul asks the question that ends that: "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" (1Co 4:7). And the Preacher reminds us that "favour to men of skill" is not guaranteed; "time and chance happeneth to them all" (Ecc 9:11). Teach your children to get very good at worthwhile things, and to say thank you to the One who made their hands.
roots_summary: Old English cracian (to make a sharp noise, to break) → cracked, broken, then crazy → c. 2018–2019 Fortnite and Twitch: cracked, extremely skilled.
roots_lines: Old English cracian — to resound, to crack
Cracked — split, broken; later, mentally unsound
Cracked up — praised ("not all it’s cracked up to be")
c. 2018–2019: Fortnite and Twitch players called cracked
Now any extreme skill: cracked at chess, at math, at piano
usage: "My little brother is cracked at Rocket League, it’s embarrassing."
God fills craftsmen with skill for His work (Exo 31:3).
What hast thou that thou didst not receive? (1Co 4:7)

etymology: From Pixar’s Inside Out (2015), in which a girl’s most important experiences are stored as glowing core memories that power the "islands" of her personality. Around 2021–2022 TikTok made "that unlocked a core memory" a stock phrase for a sight, song, or smell that brings back a formative childhood moment, and "making core memories" a caption for family outings. The sequel Inside Out 2 (2024) renewed the phrase.
biblical_def: In current slang a core memory is a formative memory — the kind that shaped who you are — and "that unlocked a core memory" means something suddenly brought one back. Parents now speak of "making core memories" with their children, and the instinct is right. The Christian observation: God builds His people by memory on purpose. Israel was commanded, "thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness" (Deu 8:2), and the stones taken from the Jordan were to "be for a memorial unto the children of Israel for ever" (Jos 4:7). The psalmist preaches to his own forgetful heart: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits" (Psa 103:2). Jeremiah, sitting in the ruins of Jerusalem, survives by memory: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope" (Lam 3:21). And the Lord Jesus gave His church a meal that is a core memory by design: "this do in remembrance of me" (Luk 22:19). The Christian does not leave core memories to chance, or to a cartoon of emotions at a control panel. A father tells his daughter: we will make memories, and the deepest ones will be of God’s faithfulness — family worship, answered prayer, the Lord’s Table — so that when trouble comes, you have something to recall to mind.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (from Pixar’s Inside Out, 2015; TikTok c. 2021–2022) for a formative memory — and God shapes His people by memory on purpose, from the Jordan stones to the Lord’s Supper.
webster_full: CORE MEMORY, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2021–present; from Inside Out, 2015) A formative memory that helped shape who one is. "Grandpa teaching me to fish is a core memory."
"That unlocked a core memory" — something brought an old memory back vividly. "Making core memories" — doing something meant to be remembered.
Older, plain sense of memory: the faculty of recalling the past; a thing remembered; the name of the dead ("of blessed memory").

Webster (1828), root word memory: “MEM'ORY, noun […] 1. The faculty of the mind by which it retains the knowledge of past events, or ideas which are past. A distinction is made between memory and recollection. memory retains past ideas without any, or with little effort; recollection implies an effort to recall ideas that are past. Memory is the purveyor of reason.”
Decode for parents: your children are telling you which moments formed them. Fill the album with God’s faithfulness.
scriptures: Deu 8:2

And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.
Jos 4:7

Then ye shall answer them, That the waters of Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD; when it passed over Jordan, the waters of Jordan were cut off: and these stones shall be for a memorial unto the children of Israel for ever.
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
Lam 3:21
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: Core memory rightly sees that memories form a person; the drift is a cartoon psychology that makes feelings the architects of the self, when Scripture makes remembering God’s works the foundation.
corruption_paragraphs: Inside Out taught a generation a picture of the soul: little emotions at a control panel, sorting memories into the islands of a personality. It is clever, and it is not the Bible’s picture. In Scripture the heart is not a committee of feelings but a moral centre that loves and trusts, and memory is a duty before it is a mood. God does not wait for a core memory to happen; He commands His people to set up memorials (Jos 4:7), rehearse His works (Deu 8:2), and keep a feast in His remembrance (Luk 22:19).

So the phrase is worth keeping and filling. Families make core memories whether they intend to or not; the only question is what they are about. A childhood full of screens remembers screens. A childhood with psalms at bedtime, a father praying through a crisis, and the Lord’s Supper taken with reverence remembers a faithful God, and that memory holds under weight: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope" (Lam 3:21). Teach your children to bless the LORD and forget not all His benefits (Psa 103:2).
roots_summary: Latin memoria (remembrance) → English memory → Pixar’s Inside Out (2015) → c. 2021–2022 TikTok: "that unlocked a core memory."
roots_lines: Latin memor — mindful; memoria, remembrance
English core — the heart of a fruit, then the centre of anything (origin uncertain)
2015: Pixar’s Inside Out — glowing core memories power a girl’s personality
c. 2021–2022 TikTok: "that unlocked a core memory," "making core memories"
2024: Inside Out 2 renews the phrase
usage: "The smell of that church basement just unlocked a core memory."
Set up stones, and tell your children what they mean (Jos 4:7).
This do in remembrance of me (Luk 22:19) — the church’s core memory.

etymology: In 2022 a Swedish Roman reenactor posting as "Gaius Flavius" urged women on Instagram to ask the men in their lives how often they think about the Roman Empire. In September 2023 the prompt went viral on TikTok, as women filmed boyfriends and husbands answering "a few times a week" or "every day." The phrase then generalized: one’s Roman Empire is any subject one thinks about constantly ("that breakup is my Roman Empire").
biblical_def: In current slang your Roman Empire is the thing you think about all the time without meaning to — a historical fascination, an old embarrassment, a song lyric, a lost friendship. It began as a joke about how often men think about Rome, and the men’s answers surprised their wives. The Christian observation: the men were onto something. Rome is not a random fixation; God set it at the centre of the story. Daniel saw a fourth kingdom "strong as iron" (Dan 2:40), and in its days "shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed" (Dan 2:44). Luke dates the birth of Christ by a Roman tax: "there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed" (Luk 2:1). Roman roads carried the gospel, and a Roman cross carried the Saviour. "When the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son" (Gal 4:4). The deeper point is the habit itself: whatever you think about constantly is shaping you, because "as he thinketh in his heart, so is he" (Pro 23:7). The blessed man has a Roman Empire too: "in his law doth he meditate day and night" (Psa 1:2). A father tells his son: think about Rome all you like — ask why God raised it and then let it fall — and make the Word of God the thing your mind returns to without being told.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Instagram 2022; TikTok trend, September 2023) for the subject one thinks about constantly — and what a man dwells on makes him (Pro 23:7), while Rome itself was God’s stage for the fulness of time (Gal 4:4).
webster_full: ROMAN EMPIRE, n. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2023–present; TikTok trend) A subject one thinks about constantly, often for no good reason. "That one awkward thing I said in seventh grade is my Roman Empire."
From the trend question "How often do you think about the Roman Empire?" Pattern: What’s your Roman Empire?
Plain historical sense: the empire ruled from Rome, from Augustus (27 BC) to the fall of the West (AD 476), and in the East to the fall of Constantinople (1453).

Webster (1828), root word empire: “EM'PIRE, noun […] 1. Supreme power in governing; supreme dominion; sovereignty; imperial power. No nation can rightfully claim the empire of the ocean. 2. The territory, region or countries under the jurisdiction and dominion of an emperor.”
Decode for parents: a light joke about fixations. Ask your children what theirs is, and tell them yours.
scriptures: Dan 2:44

And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.
Luk 2:1
And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.
Gal 4:4
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,
Pro 23:7
For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
corruption_summary: Roman Empire is a light joke about fixation; the truth beneath it is that a constant thought forms the man, so the Christian chooses his Roman Empire and makes it the law of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a reason men think about Rome. It was the greatest kingdom of iron the world had seen, and Scripture says it was raised for a purpose: in the days of those kings the God of heaven would set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed (Dan 2:44). Caesar Augustus ordered a census and moved a carpenter’s family to Bethlehem without knowing it (Luk 2:1). Roman peace, Roman roads, and a common Greek tongue across the empire were the fulness of the time (Gal 4:4). A boy fascinated by legions is close to a sermon; show him the Kingdom that outlasted them.

The trend also tells the truth about minds. Everyone has something the thoughts drift back to when nothing else demands them: a grudge, a crush, a fear, a fantasy, a game. That idle-hour subject is forming the person: "as he thinketh in his heart, so is he" (Pro 23:7). Scripture does not tell us to stop having a Roman Empire; it tells us to choose it. The blessed man’s delight is in the law of the LORD, and he meditates on it day and night (Psa 1:2). Ask your children what their Roman Empire is, and help them want a better one.
roots_summary: Latin imperium (command, rule) → Imperium Romanum → English Roman Empire → 2022 Instagram, 2023 TikTok: "How often do you think about the Roman Empire?" → one’s constant thought.
roots_lines: Latin imperium — command, sovereign rule; English empire
27 BC: Augustus, first emperor; Luke 2:1 dates the Nativity by his decree
c. 2022: a Swedish reenactor’s Instagram prompt
September 2023: TikTok trend of asking men how often they think about Rome
Generalized: my Roman Empire, any subject one thinks about constantly
usage: "The way that ref robbed us in the playoffs is my Roman Empire."
Rome was the stage for the fulness of time (Gal 4:4).
Choose your Roman Empire: meditate in His law day and night (Psa 1:2).

etymology: From hip-hop and sports slang, where cooking means producing something excellent (a producer cooking up beats in the studio; a basketball player cooking his defender). "Let him cook" — let him keep going, he is onto something — became a widespread Twitter and TikTok reply around 2022–2023, used for an unusual idea, a risky plan, or someone mid-explanation. Note the opposite: he’s cooked means he is finished.
biblical_def: In current slang let him cook means "let him keep going; he is onto something." It is said when someone has a strange idea, an unconventional plan, or a half-finished argument that others want to shout down. At bottom it is a plea for patience before judgment, and Scripture approves the instinct. "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13). "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19). The best "let him cook" in the Bible came from Gamaliel, when the council wanted to kill the apostles: "Refrain from these men, and let them alone" (Act 5:38), for "if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it" (Act 5:39). The Christian observation is that patience is not the same as approval. Paul says "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1Th 5:21) — let him cook, then taste the dish. Not every idea deserves the stove: when someone starts cooking up sin or false doctrine, the Christian does not wait to see how it turns out. A father tells his son: give people room to finish; hear them out before you mock; and when it is your turn at the stove, cook something you would be glad to serve to the Lord.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (hip-hop and sports cooking; Twitter and TikTok c. 2022–2023) for letting someone continue because he is onto something — Gamaliel’s patience (Act 5:38), held together with Paul’s "Prove all things" (1Th 5:21).
webster_full: LET HIM COOK, v. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2022–present; hip-hop and sports origin) Let him continue; he is onto something. "He wants to build a hovercraft for the science fair? Let him cook."
Variants: let her cook, let them cook; he’s cooking, he is doing well; what is he cooking?, what is he up to? Opposite: cooked, finished, doomed.
Plain older sense: to prepare food by heat; figuratively, to cook up a scheme or cook the books (falsify accounts).

Webster (1828), root word cook: “COOK, verb transitive […] 1. To prepare, as victuals for the table, by boiling, roasting, baking, broiling, etc. To dress, as meat or vegetables, for eating. 2. To prepare for any purpose. 3. To throw. […]”
Decode for parents: a call for patience with an odd idea. Teach your children to hear out, then test.
scriptures: Act 5:38
And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:
Act 5:39
But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: Let him cook is patience before judgment, which Scripture commends; its only drift is patience without testing — letting someone cook up sin because the idea is bold.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of what passes for wit among teenagers is the quick shutdown: a kid offers a strange idea and the room laughs before he finishes the sentence. Let him cook pushes back on that, and rightly. Proverbs calls answering before hearing "folly and shame" (Pro 18:13), and James wants every man "swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19). Gamaliel’s counsel saved the apostles’ lives because he was willing to wait and see whether the work was of God (Act 5:38–39).

But wait-and-see is not the whole of wisdom. Some dishes are poison from the first ingredient. When a friend is cooking up a lie, a revenge, a secret relationship, or a novel doctrine, "let him cook" is cowardice dressed as open-mindedness. Paul’s rule holds both halves together: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1Th 5:21). Hear people out; then taste, test, and say no when the dish is bad. Teach your children to be the kind of friend who listens long and judges righteously.
roots_summary: Latin coquere (to cook) → English cook → hip-hop and sports: cooking, producing something excellent → c. 2022–2023: "let him cook."
roots_lines: Latin coquere — to cook, to ripen; Old English coc, a cook
Figurative English: cook up a plan; cook the books
Hip-hop: producers cooking up beats in the studio
Sports: a player cooking a defender
c. 2022–2023 Twitter / TikTok: "let him cook"; opposite cooked
usage: "Bro is explaining his plan to start a lawn business at fourteen. Let him cook."
Hear before you answer (Pro 18:13).
Let him cook, then prove all things (1Th 5:21).

etymology: From sports and gym talk, where an athlete who recovers fast or plays through pain is "built different." The phrase spread on Twitter and TikTok around 2020–2021, often in meme form ("we are not the same, I’m built different"), for anyone exceptional by nature — from a toddler who never cries to a friend who eats gas-station sushi without consequence.
biblical_def: In current slang someone built different is exceptional by nature — tougher, smarter, more disciplined, or simply stranger than ordinary people. It is half praise and half boast: "I’m built different" means "the rules that apply to you do not apply to me." The Christian observation: Scripture affirms real differences in how God makes people. David praises God because "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14); some are given strength, some speed, some a mind for numbers. But Paul asks the question that punctures the boast: "who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" (1Co 4:7). The difference is real; the credit is God’s. And under every difference is a deep sameness: "all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23). No one is built different at the judgment. The only person truly built different is the one who has been rebuilt: "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new" (2Co 5:17). "We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works" (Eph 2:10). A father tells his daughter: you are made with care and you have gifts others do not, so use them and thank God; but never think the rules of sin and grace skip you. The new creation is the only different build that lasts.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (sports and gym talk; Twitter and TikTok c. 2020–2021) for someone exceptional by nature — a real difference God makes (Psa 139:14), a false boast when it forgets who made it (1Co 4:7), and fully true only of the new creature in Christ (2Co 5:17).
webster_full: BUILT DIFFERENT, adj. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; sports origin) Exceptional by nature; not subject to ordinary limits. "She ran the mile on a sprained ankle. Built different."
Often ironic: "I’m built different" after doing something foolish and surviving it. Related boast: "we are not the same."
Plain sense: constructed in another way, as a house or a machine.

Webster (1828), root word different: “DIFFERENT, adjective 1. Distinct; separate; not the same; as, we belong to different churches or nations. 2. Various or contrary; of various or contrary natures, forms or qualities; unlike; dissimilar; as different kinds of food or drink; different states of health; different shapes; different degrees of excellence.”
Decode for parents: praise, boast, or joke. Thank God for the real differences; puncture the boast with 1 Corinthians 4:7.
scriptures: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
Rom 3:23
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
Eph 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
corruption_summary: Built different notices real God-given differences, then turns them into a boast and an exemption; Scripture credits the Maker, levels all men under sin, and reserves the true new build for those in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: God does not make people from a template. Some children are strong, some quick, some patient, some brilliant, and David praised God for the care that went into his own frame (Psa 139:14). A boy who discovers he is unusually fast or unusually gifted at math has discovered something true. The slang goes wrong in two steps: it takes the credit ("I’m built different," as if he had built himself), and it claims an exemption (the rules for others do not apply to me). Paul’s question answers both: "who maketh thee to differ from another?" (1Co 4:7).

The exemption is the more dangerous lie. A teen who believes he is built different takes risks that kill ordinary people and expects consequences to skip him. Scripture flattens the field: "all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23). The only difference that matters at the last day is not native toughness but new birth. In Christ a man is "a new creature" (2Co 5:17), God’s own workmanship, "created in Christ Jesus unto good works" (Eph 2:10). Teach your children that they are wonderfully made, equally fallen, and invited to be made new.
roots_summary: Old English byldan (to build a house) + Latin differre (to carry apart) → sports and gym talk → c. 2020–2021 meme: "I’m built different."
roots_lines: Old English byldan — to construct a house; English build, built
Latin differre — to carry apart; English different
Sports and gym talk: an athlete "built different" in toughness or recovery
c. 2020–2021 Twitter / TikTok meme: "we are not the same"
Now praise, boast, or joke for anyone exceptional
usage: "He did his homework on the bus and still got an A. Built different."
Who maketh thee to differ? (1Co 4:7) — the build has a Builder.
The only lasting different build: a new creature in Christ (2Co 5:17).

etymology: From African American English and sports talk: "he’s him" (often written "he’s HIM") declares that a player is the real deal, the one everyone has been waiting for. It circulated on sports Twitter in the late 2010s and was everywhere by 2020–2021; the first-person boast is "I’m him." The grammar is deliberate: the bare pronoun carries the weight, as if no other description were needed.
biblical_def: In current slang he’s him means he is the real deal — the star, the one the team has been waiting for, the man who delivers when it counts. It is high praise, usually for an athlete, sometimes for a friend who came through. The Christian observation: the phrase has a startling echo in the Gospels, because the whole Bible is waiting for Him. John the Baptist sent from prison to ask Jesus, "Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?" (Mat 11:3) — in effect, is it You? Jesus told the woman at the well, "I that speak unto thee am he" (Joh 4:26). When soldiers came to arrest Him in the garden and He answered "I am he," they "went backward, and fell to the ground" (Joh 18:6). Even the anointing of David came with the words "Arise, anoint him: for this is he" (1Sa 16:12), pointing ahead to David’s greater Son. Every "he’s him" in sport is a small, passing version of a hunger only Christ satisfies: someone who finally delivers. The right response to the true Him is John the Baptist’s: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). A father tells his son: cheer for the athlete who comes through, and become a man others can count on; but there is only one Man of whom the whole creation will say at last, He is Him.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (African American English and sports Twitter, late 2010s) for someone who is the real deal — a small echo of the Bible’s great question, "Art thou he that should come" (Mat 11:3), answered by Christ: "I that speak unto thee am he" (Joh 4:26).
webster_full: HE’S HIM, phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2019–present; AAVE and sports origin) He is the real deal; the standout everyone has been waiting for. "Forty points in a playoff game. He’s him."
Forms: I’m him (a boast), she’s her, he’s not him (a letdown). Often written in capitals: HIM.
Plain grammar a grandparent will notice: him where school grammar wants he; the object pronoun used as an emphatic title.

Webster (1828), root word he: “HE, pronoun of the third person; nom. he; poss.his; obj. him. […] 1. A pronoun, a substitute for the third person, masculine gender, representing the man or male person named before. Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee. Genesis 3:16. Thou shalt fear Jehovah thy God; him shalt thou serve.”
Decode for parents: high praise for someone who delivers. Point your son to the One who always does.

corruption_summary: He’s him is honest praise for a standout; the drift is hero worship, crowning athletes and influencers with a title that, in its fullest sense, belongs only to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation looks for a man who will finally deliver: the quarterback, the general, the candidate, the influencer. Sports fans say he’s him with a kind of relief, as though the waiting is over. The relief never lasts; the star ages, gets hurt, disappoints, or falls. That repeated letdown is not an accident. Israel lived in the same longing for centuries, and John the Baptist voiced it from a prison cell: "Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?" (Mat 11:3).

Jesus answered by works and by words: "I that speak unto thee am he" (Joh 4:26). When He said "I am he" in the garden, armed men fell to the ground (Joh 18:6). Praise for a good athlete is fine; worship of him is idolatry, and teenagers drift from one to the other quickly. Teach your children John’s posture toward the true Him: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). And raise sons who come through for others, because they follow the One who never fails.
roots_summary: Old English hē, him → AAVE emphatic him → late-2010s sports Twitter: "he’s him" → Gen-Z praise for the real deal.
